summary: The article provides a largely accurate overview of Fixed Deposit taxation in India, including TDS rules, Form 15G/15H, and tax-saving FDs. However, some TDS thresholds mentioned are outdated for the current financial year (FY 2025-26).

claims.claim: Interest earned on Fixed Deposits (FDs) is fully taxable as 'Income from Other Sources' and added to your total income.
claims.note: Interest from FDs is indeed taxable under 'Income from Other Sources' as per the Income Tax Act, 1961.

claims.claim: Banks deduct Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) if your FD interest exceeds ₹40,000 (₹50,000 for senior citizens) in a financial year.
claims.note: For FY 2025-26, the TDS threshold for individuals below 60 years is ₹50,000, and for senior citizens, it is ₹1,00,000. The article's figures are for previous financial years.

claims.claim: You can submit Form 15G (for non-senior citizens) or Form 15H (for senior citizens) to avoid TDS if your total income is below the taxable limit.
claims.note: Forms 15G and 15H are indeed used for this purpose, provided the income criteria are met.

claims.claim: Certain FDs, known as 'Tax-Saving FDs,' offer deductions under Section 80C for the principal invested, but their interest remains taxable.
claims.note: Tax-saving FDs qualify for Section 80C deduction up to ₹1.5 lakh, but the interest earned is taxable.

claims.claim: The principal amount invested in these FDs, up to a maximum of ₹1.5 lakhs in a financial year, is eligible for deduction under Section 80C of the Income Tax Act, 1961.
claims.note: This is correct as per Section 80C of the Income Tax Act.

claims.claim: An additional 4% Health and Education Cess will apply to this tax.
claims.note: The Health and Education Cess is indeed 4% on the income tax payable.

claims.claim: If you have not provided your PAN, the TDS rate jumps to 20%.
claims.note: This is a correct statement regarding TDS deduction without PAN.

article_title: Fixed Deposits: Tax on FD Interest & Key Rules for Depositors
